documents.name: Approved RBI knowledge — Digital Payment Security Controls

chunks.text: Approved reference summary: RBI Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls, 2021. For payment workflows, assess strong authentication, fraud-risk management, secure application lifecycle, transaction reconciliation, logging, incident handling and relevant security testing. Confirm whether this direction or a more specific RBI direction applies to the regulated entity, payment channel, and third parties.

business objective: The system should allow customers to submit insurance claims digitally, upload supporting documents, track claim status, and receive claim decisions. It should reduce manual processing time, improve transparency for customers, and allow the organization to quickly introduce and refine claim-processing features based on user feedback and changing business requirements. users and roles: The primary users are customers, claims officers, insurance assessors, fraud investigators, compliance officers, customer support staff, and system administrators. Customers should submit claims, upload documents, and track their status. Claims officers should review and process claims.

Assessors should evaluate supporting evidence and claim validity. Fraud investigators should identify suspicious claims. Compliance officers should verify regulatory requirements. Customer support staff should handle user issues, while administrators should manage users, workflows, and system configuration. workflow and outcomes: A fraud investigation should start when predefined risk indicators are detected, such as inconsistent customer information, suspicious transaction patterns, duplicate or altered documents, unusual claim amounts or frequency, mismatched identity information, abnormal account activity, or alerts from fraud-detection systems.

The case should then be assessed using a combination of automated risk scoring, available transaction and customer data, document verification, and manual review by an authorized fraud investigator. Cases should be classified based on their risk and evidence as legitimate, suspicious and requiring further investigation, or confirmed fraudulent. The case owner should receive a clear case status, risk assessment, evidence summary, recommended action, and required next steps. Confirmed fraud should be escalated to the appropriate compliance or legal team, while legitimate cases should be cleared and the normal business workflow resumed.

All investigation decisions and actions should be recorded for audit and future improvement of the fraud-detection process. exceptions: f required information or evidence is missing, the case should be placed on hold and the case owner should be notified of the specific information required. System or fraud-detection failures should be logged, retried where appropriate, and escalated to the technical support team without losing case data or investigation history. If the evidence does not support fraud, the case should be rejected or closed as legitimate with the reason documented, and the normal business process should resume.

If fraud is confirmed, the case should be escalated according to the organization’s fraud and compliance procedures. Manual overrides should be allowed only for authorized senior fraud investigators or compliance officers, require a documented reason, and be recorded in the audit trail. The fraud investigation team owns case assessment and resolution, while compliance, legal, or technical teams own regulatory, legal, or system-related escalations. business rules: The investigation workflow should continue only when the case contains the mandatory customer information, transaction or claim details, supporting evidence, and required verification results.

Predefined risk thresholds should determine whether a case is classified as low, medium, or high risk. Low-risk cases may be cleared automatically when all required checks pass, while medium- and high-risk cases should require review by an authorized fraud investigator. Cases exceeding defined financial or risk limits, involving repeated suspicious activity, or triggering regulatory or compliance rules should require approval from a senior fraud investigator or compliance officer. A case should not be closed as legitimate or confirmed as fraud until the required evidence and verification checks are complete.

Any exception or manual override must be authorized, justified, and recorded in the audit trail. data and integrations: The system should collect customer identity details, account or policy information, transaction or claim details, timestamps, device and access information, fraud alerts, risk scores, supporting documents, investigation notes, and case decisions. Relevant information may be exchanged with internal systems such as customer/account management, transaction processing, claims management, document management, risk and fraud-detection systems, and compliance systems.

Authorized third parties may include banks or payment processors, identity-verification providers, credit or fraud-information services, and other legally permitted external data sources. Data should be exchanged securely and only when required for the investigation. If an integration is unavailable, the system should record the failure, retry automatically where appropriate, and place the affected case on hold rather than making a decision using incomplete information. The case owner and technical support team should be notified, and processing should resume when the integration becomes available or an authorized manual verification is completed and recorded.

security and compliance: You mentioned "The system should collect customer identity details, account or policy information, transaction or claim details, timestamps, device and access inf...". Which access controls, audit records, privacy obligations, fraud checks, or compliance requirements must be met? service levels and scale: The system should support at least 20,000 fraud alerts or investigation cases per day and approximately 2,000 concurrent users, with sufficient capacity to handle peak periods such as major payment events, claim surges, promotional periods, and financial year-end activity.

Normal case-management and dashboard interactions should respond within 2 seconds, while automated fraud-risk analysis should normally complete within 10 seconds when all dependent services are available. The system should target at least 99.9% availability for critical services and continuously monitor system health, processing time, and integration failures. Investigation data, evidence, and audit records should be backed up regularly. In the event of a major failure, critical services should be restored within 1 hour (RTO), with a maximum acceptable data loss of 15 minutes (RPO).

Failed transactions or investigations must be recoverable without losing evidence, duplicating cases, or creating inconsistent investigation decisions. delivery constraints: The initial working release should be delivered within 4 months using short, iterative development cycles, with usable fraud-detection and case-management features delivered incrementally rather than waiting for the complete system. The project should have a dedicated cross-functional team consisting of developers, UI/UX designers, QA engineers, fraud analysts, security specialists, compliance experts, and business stakeholders.

Fraud investigators and compliance officers should be available frequently to review prototypes, test workflows, and provide rapid feedback. The solution depends on transaction-processing systems, customer/account databases, claims systems, identity-verification services, fraud-detection services, and other external data providers. Requirements should remain flexible during development, allowing changes based on stakeholder feedback, user testing, emerging fraud patterns, and regulatory needs. Changes should be evaluated quickly and incorporated into subsequent iterations without requiring the entire project to restart.

Reusable components and existing integrations should be preferred to reduce development time and cost. validation and rollout: The system should be tested continuously during each short development iteration using unit testing, integration testing, functional testing, security testing, and user acceptance testing. Working prototypes should be demonstrated to fraud investigators, compliance officers, and other stakeholders at the end of each iteration, with their feedback used to refine the next version. Before production, the complete system should undergo performance, security, compliance, and end-to-end testing, followed by formal stakeholder approval.

A limited pilot should then be released to a small group of users and monitored for detection accuracy, false positives, processing time, usability, and system stability. After successful pilot validation, the system should be released incrementally to a larger user base. After launch, system performance, fraud-detection accuracy, false-positive rates, security events, user feedback, and business outcomes should be continuously monitored. Improvements and new fraud-detection rules should be prioritized based on real-world feedback and delivered through short development iterations, with each change quickly tested and validated before release.

factors.name: Requirement stability
factors.rationale: All requirements have an explicit approval status.

factors.name: Requirement clarity
factors.rationale: Measured from the presence of concrete, non-placeholder acceptance criteria.

factors.name: Risk
factors.rationale: Derived from stated high risk and security, privacy, regulatory, or audit classifications.

factors.name: Complexity
factors.rationale: Integration and data-management requirements increase coordination and technical complexity.

factors.name: Need for early prototype
factors.rationale: Unclear requirements or integration complexity make early learning and validation valuable.

factors.name: Time constraints
factors.rationale: No schedule or deadline evidence is available in the generated requirements; confirm this with the project sponsor.

factors.name: Customer involvement
factors.rationale: Derived only from business, stakeholder, or usability requirements; otherwise this must be confirmed.

factors.name: Frequency of changes
factors.rationale: Requirement documents do not establish the expected change rate; confirm with product and business stakeholders.

factors.name: Need for iterative development
factors.rationale: Unapproved or unclear requirements benefit from repeated review and validation cycles.

factors.name: Need for risk analysis
factors.rationale: Security/compliance concerns or complex integration warrant explicit risk analysis.

options.name: Spiral
options.suitability: Best when risk analysis, prototypes, and repeated risk-reduction cycles are central.

options.name: Prototyping
options.suitability: Best for validating uncertain user needs, workflows, and interfaces before committing to a full build.

options.name: Agile
options.suitability: Best for frequent feedback and evolving requirements, with planned governance for high-risk work.

options.name: DevSecOps
options.suitability: Best where iterative delivery is paired with automated security, assurance, and operational controls.

options.name: Incremental
options.suitability: Best when value can be divided into validated, independently testable increments.

options.name: Agile–V-Model hybrid
options.suitability: Best where evolving delivery needs formal verification and validation gates for regulated scope.

options.name: V-Shape
options.suitability: Best when each specification stage needs a linked verification and validation activity.

options.name: Waterfall
options.suitability: Best when requirements are stable, fully specified, and changes are controlled.

options.name: RAD
options.suitability: Best for time-boxed delivery with available users and modular, lower-risk scope.

sdlc.justification: Spiral has the highest transparent score because requirement stability is baseline approved, requirement clarity is low, risk is high, complexity is high, need for early prototype is likely. Factors marked 'Not evidenced' are deliberately neutral and require stakeholder confirmation before the SDLC is approved.
